title: Serbia leads Electricity Integration Package transposition, but coupling still not reached
programme: Energy Community Electricity Integration Package (market coupling)
problem: Until its market is coupled with the EU day-ahead and intraday markets, Serbia cannot qualify for the CBAM exemption for electricity.
solution: Serbia adopted a comprehensive set of primary and secondary acts to fully transpose the Electricity Integration Package, the legal basis for joining EU market coupling. The Secretariat and the European Commission must then verify compliance.
funding: The EU Reform and Growth Facility for the Western Balkans ties its support to binding deadlines for adopting this legislation.
results: As of 9 September 2025 Serbia had day-ahead and intraday markets running and its transposition framework adopted, but compliance was not yet verified. No Contracting Party met the 31 December 2023 deadline and none is expected to join EU market coupling before 2027, so CBAM applies from 1 January 2026.
serbia_reason: This is Serbia's own path to the CBAM exemption: it is closest to the 'point of no return', but after that the pace depends on EU bodies. Growth Facility deadlines add EU funding conditionality to the legal obligation.
adapt_needed: Serbia needs to submit complete laws with good-quality English concordance tables quickly, so that the Secretariat and Commission verification and the 18-month technical preparation can start.
blockers: Verification of the transposition, approval of the market coupling integration plan by ACER and the stalled Shadow SEE capacity calculation region, held up by the Serbia–Kosovo dispute, are outside Serbia's control or politically hard.
quote: Considering the current status of fulfilment of the market coupling preconditions, it is highly unlikely that any Contracting Party will be able to join SDAC and SIDC before 2027. Consequently, CBAM payments are expected to apply from 1 January 2026 to electricity imports from Contracting Parties into the EU.

title: Serbia cut SO2 sharply yet still breaches Large Combustion Plant ceilings
programme: Energy Community Large Combustion Plants Directive – National Emission Reduction Plan (NERP)
problem: Serbia's lignite power plants emit SO2 and NOx above the ceilings that have applied under Energy Community law since 1 January 2018.
solution: Serbia applies the Large Combustion Plants Directive through a National Emission Reduction Plan with falling emission ceilings, while some units ran under an opt-out regime that expired at the end of 2023.
implementer: Government of Serbia and thermal power plant operators
delivery_partners: Energy Community Secretariat (monitoring and dispute settlement)
results: In 2024 Serbia significantly reduced SO2 and kept within its dust ceiling, but SO2 compliance remains out of reach. The opted-out Morava plant and the three Kolubara A3 units were still operating after the opt-out expired.
serbia_reason: Serbia's own lignite fleet is failing a binding Energy Community obligation. The Secretariat adds that CBAM will further erode generators' revenues, raising doubts about keeping such plants open.
adapt_needed: Serbia needs a plant-by-plant decision to retrofit or close, taking account of the rising fuel use from pollution controls and of CBAM costs.
blockers: Retrofits need substantial capital and raise fuel use and CO2 emissions, while coal plants are seen as critical for system adequacy.
quote: North Macedonia and Serbia reduced their SO 2 emissions—Serbia significantly—yet compliance with the ceilings remains out of reach. Combined with the gradual lowering of the ceilings, this suggests that breaches are likely to become more severe in the coming years.

title: Serbia's NECP sets 2050 coal exit while adding new lignite unit
programme: Serbia NECP and Just Transition Plan
problem: Serbia's power system relies on lignite, and no Contracting Party has written a coal phase-out into domestic law.
solution: Serbia's adopted NECP plans to cut lignite use by up to 25% by 2030 compared with 2019 and indicates a 2050 coal phase-out. A Just Transition Plan is under consultation.
delivery_partners: Energy Community Secretariat (Policy Guidelines on Just Transition)
results: The 350 MW Kostolac B3 lignite unit was commissioned at the end of 2024, taking Serbia's lignite capacity to over 4.3 GW. Serbia is not a Powering Past Coal Alliance member, while North Macedonia plans to convert its coal plants by 2027.
serbia_reason: Serbia's coal exit plan sits inside its Energy Community NECP and just-transition obligations, and the Secretariat cites 2050 as an example of a far-off date. Adding lignite capacity works against the plan's direction.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need a plant-by-plant closure timetable and a finalised Just Transition Plan instead of a single distant end date.
blockers: Coal still supplies a large share of electricity and new lignite capacity has just been commissioned, so there is pressure to keep using it.
quote: However, North Macedonia and Ukraine have included fixed coal phase-out dates in their adopted national planning documents. The Serbian NECP indicates a coal phase-out date of 2050 in the energy mix and the Serbian Just Transition Plan is currently under consultation.

title: Serbia's second renewables auction awarded 424.8 MW of solar and wind
problem: Serbia must raise the renewable share of its energy use to meet its 2030 Energy Community target.
solution: Serbia held a second renewable energy auction and added qualification criteria that reward bidders offering a share of their capacity to the guaranteed supplier or directly to end-users.
results: The round awarded 424.8 MW of solar and wind projects, with expected installed capacity of up to 650 MW. The source says the new criteria let more projects benefit under the quota and promote renewable PPAs.
serbia_reason: This is Serbia's own auction design, used to meet its Energy Community renewables target. The extra criterion is an innovation neighbours could copy.
adapt_needed: Future rounds would need grid capacity and balancing arrangements to match the larger expected installed capacity.
blockers: Regulated retail prices and limited market liquidity weaken the business case for renewable PPAs.
quote: Serbia has completed its second renewable energy auction, awarding 424.8 MW of solar and wind projects, with an expected installation capacity of up to 650 MW. A key innovation in this round was the introduction of additional qualification criteria based on the share of capacity offered to the guaranteed supplier or directly to end-users.

title: Serbia completes MRVA transposition and issues about 100 GHG permits
programme: Monitoring, reporting, verification and accreditation (MRVA) of GHG emissions
problem: Without verified installation-level emissions data, Serbia can neither run a credible carbon price nor show compatibility with the EU framework.
solution: Serbia transposed the core EU ETS Directive provisions and the EU monitoring, reporting, accreditation and verification rules, and began issuing GHG permits and approving monitoring plans. This obligation is also written into the Western Balkan Reform Agendas.
funding: Progress on MRVA is a condition for EU support under the Reform and Growth Facility of the Growth Plan for the Western Balkans.
results: Serbia has completed transposition and approximately 100 GHG permits have been issued. The National Accreditation Body is preparing to review the first applications from verifiers.
serbia_reason: This is Serbia's own groundwork for a domestic carbon price; the Secretariat calls MRVA the backbone of any emissions trading scheme. EU Growth Plan funding conditions helped drive it.
adapt_needed: Serbia now needs working accreditation and verified annual emission reports before a carbon tax or ETS can rely on the data.
blockers: Building the procedural and institutional framework is described as a major challenge for public authorities and operators.
quote: In Serbia, the transposition process has been completed; entities subject to the new obligations are preparing applications for the approval of GHG permits and monitoring plans and approximately 100 GHG permits have already been issued. The National Accreditation Body is preparing to review the first applications for accreditation submitted by verifiers.

title: Serbia plans low carbon tax from 2027, later a fixed-price ETS
programme: Serbia carbon tax with later fixed-price ETS
problem: Emissions from electricity generation in Serbia are unpriced, so EU importers pay the full CBAM charge on electricity from Serbia.
solution: Serbia plans to introduce a carbon tax in 2027 that could later evolve into a national fixed-price ETS.
results: The planned start price is 4 EUR/tCO2eq, rising to 40 EUR/tCO2eq in 2030, against an EU ETS average of EUR 56.63 per tonne in 2024. The Secretariat judges that the moderate prices planned across the region are unlikely to substantially reduce CBAM payments from 2026.
serbia_reason: This is Serbia's own carbon pricing plan, designed with an eye on the CBAM exemption conditions. The low starting price limits how much CBAM cost it can offset.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need a faster price path and coordination with neighbours on timing, coverage or a minimum price to avoid trade distortions.
blockers: A higher carbon price would raise costs for lignite generation and regulated tariffs.
quote: North Macedonia and Moldova are considering introducing a carbon tax, while Serbia plans to implement a carbon tax that could later evolve into a national fixed-price ETS.

title: Regulated household tariffs shield consumers but strain public utilities
problem: State intervention keeps household electricity prices far below EU levels, so consumers do not see wholesale or CBAM-driven cost changes.
solution: Serbia and several neighbours have been gradually raising regulated household prices towards market-based supply costs.
results: Household prices excluding taxes rose 9.29% in Serbia in 2024, yet household prices across the Contracting Parties stayed at about one-third of the EU-27 average. Serbia's industrial prices stayed stable and closer to EU levels.
serbia_reason: Serbia's retail price shield is paid for mainly by public utilities or the state budget. The Secretariat warns that it delays adaptation to CBAM and to market integration.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need to keep moving tariffs towards cost, with targeted protection for vulnerable households instead of a general price shield.
blockers: Raising household electricity prices is politically sensitive.
quote: As a result, the financial impacts of CBAM-driven changes in cross-border trade are unlikely to be felt directly by these groups. However, this insulation delays or prevents corrective and adaptation measures, increasing vulnerability and placing additional financial strain on the entities providing the price shield—primarily public utilities or state budgets.

title: CBAM default rules risk charging EU power that only transits Serbia
problem: Electricity imports are assigned to the last non-EU country they pass through, and default emission factors apply regardless of where the power was generated.
solution: The EU applies CBAM to electricity imports from 1 January 2026, using fossil-based default emission factors unless strict conditions for using actual emissions are met.
results: Serbia carried 9,181 GWh of scheduled flows to the EU in 2024, mostly transit, implying CBAM exposure for EU importers of over EUR 612 million as an upper-bound estimate. Market participants consider the conditions for using actual emissions almost impossible to meet.
serbia_reason: As the region's main transit corridor, Serbia carries the largest estimated CBAM exposure, even for electricity generated in EU member states. Recognition of transit flows matters more for Serbia than for any neighbour.
adapt_needed: Serbia would need systems that verify the true origin of electricity flowing through its grid.
blockers: Identifying transit becomes practically impossible on anonymous, liquid exchanges, and fixing the default values requires amending the EU Regulation, unlikely before 2027.
quote: This poses the serious risk that EU importers will face CBAM charges on electricity that may have originated from another EU Member State, simply because it passed through a Contracting Party. This issue is particularly relevant in the Western Balkans, where most Contracting Parties act primarily as transit corridors rather than consistent exporters, as explained in the chapter on electricity trade.
